concepts.title: Habits
concepts.hook: Missing one day did not undo a new habit in Lally's 12-week study. Habits were estimated to take from 18 to 254 days to settle in.
concepts.rule: A cue can start a learned act. Repeating it in the same place makes the link stronger. In Lally's study, habits took very different times to settle, and one missed day did not undo them.

claims.text: Cues in a stable setting, like a place or an act just before, can bring back a learned action with little thought.
In Lally's 84-day study, the estimated time to near full habit strength ranged from 18 to 254 days, and one missed chance did not undo habit growth.
In that study, half of the 39 people whose data fit the curve well took more than 66 days to reach near full habit strength.
Early repeats in the same setting add the most to how automatic an act feels; later repeats add less and less.
Students who moved to a new university kept old habits mainly when parts of the old setting stayed the same.
Lally's team notes that in an earlier study, missing a whole week, unlike one day, made later practice less likely.

items.stem: Kunal opens his flashcard app each time his train pulls out of Dadar. This week he takes a bus instead. What is most likely?

options.text: He opens it as usual, since he still wants to revise.
options.feedback: Wanting to revise is not the same as the cue. Without the train, the act is less likely.

options.text: He forgets the app more often.
options.feedback: With the train gone, the cue is gone too, so the app is easier to forget.

options.text: He opens it more, to make up for it.
options.feedback: A missing cue makes the act less likely, not more.

items.stem: Ishaan thinks pure willpower drives his evening sit-ups. Yet he does them only right after the TV goes off. Why does that point to a cue?

options.text: Willpower is strongest just after watching TV.
options.feedback: Nothing shows willpower peaks then. The fixed moment is the sign of a cue.

options.text: His goal to exercise matters more than the TV cue.
options.feedback: A goal may not start a habit when its cue is absent. The TV going off is the cue here.

options.text: The act follows the same moment each time.
options.feedback: When an act always comes right after one moment, that moment is working as a cue.

items.stem: Put the growth of Rehan's after-dinner guitar habit in order.

options.text: Dinner ends, and that becomes his cue to play.
options.feedback: The cue comes first: the end of dinner starts the act.

options.text: The first weeks of playing bring big gains in ease.
options.feedback: Early repeats in the same setting add the most.

options.text: Later weeks add smaller and smaller gains.
options.feedback: As the curve nears its plateau, each repeat adds less.

options.text: Playing after dinner now needs little thought.
options.feedback: Near the plateau, the cue starts the act almost by itself.

items.stem: In the hostel, Pia's new push-up habit still gets easier each day. Raj's push-ups barely change any more. Working back from that, whose habit is likely older?

options.text: Raj's, since gains level off later on.
options.feedback: Right. Early repeats bring big jumps and later ones add little, so a habit that barely changes is further along.

options.text: Pia's, since big daily gains mean a long run.
options.feedback: Big daily gains come early. A habit that still jumps each day is most likely the newer one.

options.text: Neither; gains look the same at any age.
options.feedback: Repeats add the most early and less later, so the size of the daily gain hints at a habit's age.

items.stem: In Lally’s 12-week habit study, half of people took more than about how many days for an act to feel automatic?

options.text: About 66 days.
options.feedback: Right. Half of people took more than about 66 days, though single people ranged from 18 to 254.

options.text: About 30 days.
options.feedback: Thirty days is too short. In the study, half of people took more than about 66 days, over two months.

options.text: About 254 days.
options.feedback: That was the longest estimate. Half of people took more than about 66 days.

items.stem: Missing one day did little harm to Neel's morning jog. Then exams make him skip a full week. Why could this gap matter more?

options.text: A habit resets to zero after any single miss, big or small.
options.feedback: One missed day did not undo habit growth, so a reset after any miss is wrong.

options.text: A week of missed chances can hold a habit back.
options.feedback: One miss did little harm in the study, but a whole week off made later practice less likely in earlier work.

options.text: One missed day resets the habit, so a week adds no harm.
options.feedback: One missed chance did not erase habit growth. A whole week off made later practice less likely.

misconceptions.name: One fixed day count
misconceptions.correction: Habit time varies by person and act; there is no fixed day count.

misconceptions.name: One miss resets all
misconceptions.correction: One missed chance did not wipe out habit growth in the study.

misconceptions.name: Goal replaces cue
misconceptions.correction: A steady goal may not start a habit when a usual cue is gone.

misconceptions.name: Every repeat adds the same
misconceptions.correction: Early repeats add the most; later repeats add less and less.

steps.title: A cue starts a habit

hook.stem: Why do many people grab their phone the moment they get home?

options.text: Getting home sets it off.
options.feedback: Right. Walking in the door is the cue, so the phone comes out with little thought.

options.text: They decide to, every single time.
options.feedback: A habit needs little deciding. The cue of getting home starts it.

options.text: Phones send more alerts in the evening.
options.feedback: Alerts can play a part, but the habit is set off by getting home.

steps.teach: A habit often starts with a cue: a place, a time or an act just before it. The cue sets the act off, so you barely decide.

parts: After brushing his teeth,
Arun drops to the bedroom floor
and does ten push-ups.
example.spot: After brushing his teeth,
example.feedback: Brushing his teeth comes first each time, so it is the cue for the push-ups.

guided.stem: Ravi wants to study at home too, but he studies well only at the library desk. What might home be missing?
guided.hint: Which thing is only in one place?

options.text: The desk cue.
options.feedback: Right. The library desk is a cue that his home does not have.

options.text: His wish to study.
options.feedback: He wants to study in both places. The setting is what differs.

options.text: More deciding, since habits run on fresh choices.
options.feedback: With a cue, you barely decide. The library desk sets off studying, and home has no such cue.

guided.stem: Each morning Priyanka puts the kettle on, then checks her plant pots without thinking. The kettle breaks, so she boils water in a pan. By night the plants are unchecked. Why?
guided.hint: What came just before the pot check each day?

options.text: Putting the kettle on was the cue, and it changed.
options.feedback: Right. The kettle was the act just before the check. With the cue gone, the check did not start by itself.

options.text: Her wish to look after the plants faded.
options.feedback: Her wish did not change in a day. The cue changed, and a goal alone may not start a habit.

options.text: She chose to skip it, as habits run on daily choice.
options.feedback: A habit needs little choosing. The kettle cue set the check off, and that cue was missing.

guided.stem: At her new office in Kochi, Deepa eats a biscuit each time she opens her late-morning email batch. She hardly notices doing it. What is most likely starting the snack?
guided.hint: What happens just before the biscuit every day?

options.text: Hunger that builds up by late morning.
options.feedback: Hunger may play a part, but the snack comes with the emails each time. That fixed moment acts as the cue.

options.text: Opening the emails at that time.
options.feedback: Right. The snack comes with the emails each time, so that fixed moment is working as a cue.

options.text: A fresh daily choice.
options.feedback: She hardly notices it, which points to a cue. A habit set off by a cue needs little deciding.

steps.takeaway: Find the cue, and you find what starts the habit.

steps.title: Early repeats count most

hook.stem: Week one of a new routine or week ten: when does each day of practice add more?

options.text: In week one.
options.feedback: Right. Early repeats bring the biggest jumps in how easy the act feels.

options.text: In week ten.
options.feedback: By week ten the gains are small. The big jumps come early.

options.text: Every week adds the same.
options.feedback: In one study the gains shrank over time, so the weeks were not equal.

steps.teach: Each repeat in the same setting makes the act more automatic. Early repeats add the most, and later ones add less, so the gains level off.

parts: In week one, Sana's morning walk goes from hard to fairly easy,
in week six it gets a little easier,
and by week ten it barely changes.
example.spot: In week one, Sana's morning walk goes from hard to fairly easy,
example.feedback: The first week brings the biggest change, because early repeats add the most.

guided.stem: Asha's rope routine now starts without effort. She wants a new stretching habit. Should she expect that one to begin fully automatic?
guided.hint: Ask where a brand-new act sits on the curve.

options.text: No, it needs its own early repeats.
options.feedback: Right. Each act climbs its own curve, so the stretching starts at the steep early part, not at the top.

options.text: Yes, her rope habit carries over to it.
options.feedback: Her rope routine got easy through its own repeats. A new act has had none yet, so it starts low.

options.text: No, and each day will add the same amount.
options.feedback: It does start low, but the gains are not even. Early repeats add the most, then the gains level off.

guided.stem: Mitali has practised sitar after school for two months, and it now feels almost automatic. If she keeps going one more week, what will that week most likely add?
guided.hint: Where on the curve is she now?

options.text: The biggest jump yet, as practice piles up.
options.feedback: Gains do not grow with time. Early repeats add the most, and later ones add less.

options.text: Week one's gain.
options.feedback: The first week brought the big jump. Near the plateau, a week adds much less.

options.text: A small gain in ease.
options.feedback: Right. She is near the plateau, where each repeat adds less and less.

guided.stem: Joseph joins a bank in Chennai and must learn a new billing screen. In week one his speed jumped. Now, months later, it barely moves. What does the flat stretch most likely mean?
guided.hint: Which part of the curve is flat?

options.text: He is close to the point where gains level off.
options.feedback: Right. Early repeats add the most and later ones add little, so a flat stretch is normal.

options.text: He is now fully trained, and his gains are done.
options.feedback: Gains do not stop dead. Later repeats still add a little, just less and less.

options.text: Each day should add the same, so he slipped back.
options.feedback: Days do not add the same. Early repeats bring big gains, and later ones add less and less.

steps.takeaway: Early repeats build a habit most; later ones add less.

steps.title: Weeks, not a fixed count, and one miss is fine

hook.stem: A poster says every habit takes exactly 21 days. Is that right?

options.text: No, it varies a lot.
options.feedback: Right. In one study the time ranged from a few weeks to many months.

options.text: Yes, 21 days for everyone.
options.feedback: No single count fits everyone. In one study times varied widely.

options.text: It takes about one week.
options.feedback: One week is too short for most people in the study.

steps.teach: Habits took an estimated 18 to 254 days to become automatic; half took over 66. One missed day did no harm, so slips are fine; a missed week can hurt.

visual.label: Estimated days until a habit felt automatic, in one 12-week study

example.ask: Tap how the run felt after the miss.
parts: Meena missed her morning run once,
went out again the next day,
and the run still felt automatic.
example.spot: and the run still felt automatic.
example.feedback: One missed day did not wipe out weeks of practice, so her run stayed automatic. Missing a whole week is riskier.

guided.stem: Kiran has meditated daily for three weeks, but it still takes effort. What does this show?
guided.hint: Compare three weeks with how long half of people took.

options.text: It can take a couple of months.
options.feedback: Right. In one study, half of people took more than 66 days, about two months.

options.text: Habits take 21 days, so his should be automatic by now.
options.feedback: There is no fixed 21 days. In one study it took 18 to 254 days, and half of people took more than 66.

options.text: The usual 21 days are up, so it will not form.
options.feedback: There is no fixed 21 days. In one study the middle time was about two months.

guided.stem: Nitin and his sister start new daily habits on the same day. After a month hers feels automatic and his does not. What fits the study?
guided.hint: Did everyone in the study need the same number of days?

options.text: His habit has failed, as a month is the limit.
options.feedback: There is no set limit. Some people took many months for a habit to feel automatic.

options.text: A gap like that is normal; times varied a lot.
options.feedback: Right. Estimated times ran from 18 to 254 days, so two people can be far apart.

options.text: Hers cannot be a real habit so soon.
options.feedback: Some habits settled in about 18 days. A month can be enough for some people and acts.

guided.stem: Hetal, a shop owner in Surat, has opened his ledger app each evening for two months. A power cut makes him miss one evening. His nephew says the habit is broken and must restart from day one. What fits the study?
guided.hint: What did one skipped day do in the study?

options.text: The nephew is right; one miss restarts the count.
options.feedback: One missed chance did not wipe out habit growth in the study, so there is no restart.

options.text: The miss is harmless just because he is two months in.
options.feedback: In the study, one missed chance did not undo habit growth. That finding was not tied to being two months in.

options.text: One missed evening did not undo the growth so far.
options.feedback: Right. In the study, one missed chance did not undo habit growth, so he can just carry on.

steps.takeaway: Give it weeks, and do not worry about one missed day.

concepts.title: Loss aversion
concepts.hook: In choice studies, people often act as if losing ₹100 counts for more than winning ₹100.
concepts.rule: Loss aversion is a pattern in choices: people act as if a loss counts for more than a same-size gain, about twice on average. It depends on the start point, and it is a tendency, not a law for every person.

claims.text: Gains and losses are judged from a reference point, which is often where you start or what you expected.
A loss tends to weigh more than a gain of the same size, so most people turn down a fair 50-50 chance to win or lose the same amount, more so as the stake grows.
Across 607 estimates from 150 papers, a loss weighed about twice a gain of the same size, on average. The figures varied from study to study.

items.stem: Tanmay can swap his ₹500 match ticket for a friend's ticket to another match he would enjoy just as much. He refuses, in case the swap turns out worse. What is pulling on him?

options.text: A possible loss counts for more than the same gain.
options.feedback: Right. In choices, the chance of ending up worse counts for more than the chance of ending up better, so he refuses an even swap.

options.text: His starting ticket cannot shape how the swap feels.
options.feedback: Choices are judged from a start point. His ticket makes a possible loss feel weightier.

options.text: A loss and a gain of one size count the same for him.
options.feedback: If they counted the same, an even swap would not bother him. In choices, a possible loss usually weighs more.

items.stem: Why do more people refuse a fair, even-chance trade when ₹10,000 is at stake than when ₹10 is?

options.text: The gain and loss feel equal at both stakes.
options.feedback: A loss tends to weigh more than an equal gain. That can matter more as the stake grows.

options.text: Dislike of fair trades grows as the stake grows.
options.feedback: The pull of a possible loss gets stronger with a bigger stake, so more people say no.

options.text: The loss weighs twice as much for each person at either stake.
options.feedback: Twice was an average across studies, not a fixed feeling for each person. Larger possible losses can deter more people.

items.stem: Ananya says her ₹400 pocket money this month feels like a cut. What was most likely true before?

options.text: She used to get less than ₹400.
options.feedback: Then ₹400 would feel like a rise, not a cut.

options.text: Prices in the shop went down.
options.feedback: Lower prices would make her money go further, not feel like a cut.

options.text: She used to get more than ₹400.
options.feedback: A result feels like a loss when it sits below the start, so her old amount was higher.

items.stem: A college fest has two notices: “Register early and save ₹100” and “Register late and pay ₹100 more.” The price gap is the same. Which notice likely pushes more students to sign up early?

options.text: The pay-more notice, which frames it as a loss.
options.feedback: The same ₹100 framed as a loss from the early price tends to weigh more than a saving.

options.text: The save notice, since saving feels best.
options.feedback: Savings are gains, and gains tend to weigh less than losses of the same size.

options.text: Neither, since the gap is the same.
options.feedback: The money gap is the same, but the start point in the wording changes how it feels.

items.stem: Pooled across many papers, about how many times as much as a same-size gain did a loss weigh, on average?

options.text: About 2 times.
options.feedback: Right. Pooled across studies, a loss weighed about twice a gain of the same size, on average.

options.text: About 1 time, the same.
options.feedback: If they weighed the same, people would happily take fair 50/50 trades. On average a loss weighed about twice as much.

options.text: About 10 times.
options.feedback: That is far too high. The pooled average was about twice, though single studies differed.

items.stem: Your cousin hears that losses weigh twice as much, and says this holds for every person in every choice. Which reply fits best?

options.text: It holds for each person, since many studies agree.
options.feedback: Many studies were pooled, but their figures differed, so it is an average.

options.text: It is false, since some studies found less.
options.feedback: Some found less and some more. The average still came out near two.

options.text: It is an average across studies, and people vary.
options.feedback: Studies gave different figures, so twice is a middle value, not a fixed rule for each person.

misconceptions.name: Equal feel
misconceptions.correction: Equal gain and loss can have a different felt weight.

misconceptions.name: Always true
misconceptions.correction: The pattern does not fix how every person will feel.

misconceptions.name: Wording never matters
misconceptions.correction: The same result can feel like a gain or a loss, depending on the start point it is framed from.

misconceptions.name: One differing study disproves the average
misconceptions.correction: Some studies found less and some found more, while the pooled average was about twice a gain.

steps.title: A loss feels bigger than a gain

hook.stem: You hold a ₹100 movie voucher. A friend offers to swap it for a 50/50 chance at a ₹200 voucher or nothing. Do most people swap?

options.text: No, most keep the voucher.
options.feedback: Right. Most people keep it, because losing the ₹100 voucher weighs more than gaining ₹100 more.

options.text: Yes, since the deal is fair.
options.feedback: It is fair on paper, but most people still say no to it.

options.text: Just people who rarely watch films say no.
options.feedback: It is not about films. Most people keep the voucher they already hold.

steps.teach: In choices, a loss tends to count more than a same-size gain, so most people turn down a fair 50/50 swap. Bigger stakes bring more refusals.

example.ask: Tap the choice the loss shaped.
parts: Sahil could trade his ₹50 food coupon
for an even chance at ₹100 or nothing,
but he keeps the coupon he has.
example.spot: but he keeps the coupon he has.
example.feedback: The chances are even, yet he keeps it, because losing his ₹50 coupon counts for more in his choice.

guided.stem: Under a made-up rule, a re-marked exam is as likely to gain 5 marks as to drop 5. Will most students ask for a re-mark?
guided.hint: Think about how people treat even chances of gain and loss.

options.text: Probably not; losing 5 marks weighs more.
options.feedback: Right. In choices, losing 5 marks counts for more than gaining 5, so most would not ask.

options.text: Yes, since the chances are even.
options.feedback: It is fair on paper, but most people still turn down even chances like this, because the loss counts for more.

options.text: Yes, winning 5 and losing 5 feel the same.
options.feedback: On paper they are equal, but in choices a loss usually counts for more.

guided.stem: Aditya finds a ₹200 note on the road in the morning and loses a ₹200 note in the evening. His cash ends the day even. How does the day most likely feel?
guided.hint: Which of the two events weighs more?

options.text: A bit worse than even.
options.feedback: Right. A loss tends to weigh more than a gain of the same size, so the day feels slightly down.

options.text: About even, since the sums match.
options.feedback: The sums match, but the feelings do not. A loss tends to count for more than a same-size gain.

options.text: A bit better, since the find came first.
options.feedback: Order was not the point. A loss tends to weigh more than a same-size gain, so the day tilts down.

guided.stem: Kartik, a farmer near Nashik, is offered an even chance that his crop price lands ₹2,000 above or below a fixed contract. Next year the same deal is ₹20,000 either way. When is he more likely to say no?
guided.hint: How does the size of the sum change people's choices?

options.text: With the smaller one.
options.feedback: It runs the other way. Refusals of fair even-chance deals grow as the stake gets bigger.

options.text: With the bigger stake.
options.feedback: Right. People turn down fair even-chance deals more often as the stake grows.

options.text: Equally often.
options.feedback: Even odds do not make the feelings even. A loss weighs more, and more so at bigger stakes.

steps.takeaway: A loss tends to feel bigger than a gain of the same size.

steps.title: It depends on where you start

hook.stem: Riya hoped for ₹500 from her aunt and got ₹300. Manoj hoped for nothing and got ₹300. Who feels better?

options.text: Manoj.
options.feedback: Right. Manoj got more than he hoped for, so ₹300 feels like a gain.

options.text: Riya.
options.feedback: Riya got less than she hoped for, so ₹300 feels like a loss to her.

options.text: Both feel the same, since both got ₹300.
options.feedback: The money is the same, but each one judges it against a different start.

steps.teach: We judge a result against where we start or what we expect. So the same ₹300 can feel like a gain to one person and a loss to another.

parts: Meghna and Wasim both end the month with ₹1,000, but
Meghna started with ₹1,500,
so her month feels like a loss.
example.spot: Meghna started with ₹1,500,
example.feedback: Her start point was higher than where she ended, so the same ₹1,000 feels like a loss.

guided.stem: One canteen says “Pay ₹5 extra by card.” Another says “Get ₹5 off with cash.” The prices end up the same. What differs?
guided.hint: Work out what you pay at each counter.

options.text: Just the start point in the wording.
options.feedback: Right. The costs match. Only the starting price in the words changes.

options.text: The real cost.
options.feedback: The real cost is the same at both. The wording sets a different start.

options.text: No difference that could change how it feels.
options.feedback: The cost matches, but the wording sets a different start, so ₹5 extra feels like a loss and ₹5 off like a gain.

guided.stem: Jatin's shares rose from ₹10,000 to ₹14,000, then fell to ₹12,000. He is still ₹2,000 up on what he paid, yet he feels he lost money. Why?
guided.hint: What number is he comparing with now?

options.text: He is below what he first put in.
options.feedback: He put in ₹10,000 and holds ₹12,000, so he is up. The feeling comes from his new start point.

options.text: Feelings follow the final total, not a start point.
options.feedback: The same total can feel like a gain or a loss. It depends on the point he compares it with.

options.text: He now judges from the ₹14,000 high point.
options.feedback: Right. His start point moved to the high, so the drop to ₹12,000 feels like a loss.

guided.stem: Before appraisals at their Pune office, Rekha was told to expect a 10% raise and Faisal was told 3%. Both get 6%. Who more likely feels the raise as a loss?
guided.hint: What did each one expect going in?

options.text: Rekha.
options.feedback: Right. She judged 6% against an expected 10%, so it falls short and can feel like a loss.

options.text: Faisal.
options.feedback: Faisal expected 3%, so 6% is above his start point. It likely feels like a gain to him.

options.text: Neither, since 6% is the same for anyone.
options.feedback: The same raise can feel different. Each person judges it against what they expected.

steps.takeaway: Gain or loss depends on where you start.

steps.title: About twice, on average

hook.stem: If a loss weighs more than a gain, by how much, on average?

options.text: About twice as much.
options.feedback: Right. Pooled over many studies, a loss weighed about twice a gain.

options.text: About ten times as much.
options.feedback: That is far too big. The pooled figure was about twice.

options.text: Just a little, about 5% more.
options.feedback: The gap was bigger than that. On average a loss weighed about twice.

steps.teach: Across many studies, a loss weighed about twice a same-size gain, on average. Estimates vary from study to study, so no one person is fixed at exactly two.

visual.label: How much a loss weighs, compared with a gain

example.ask: Tap the part about studies differing.
parts: Pooled over many studies, losses weighed about twice as much,
but the figures differed from study to study,
so the twice is an average.
example.spot: but the figures differed from study to study,
example.feedback: The studies did not all agree, so twice is a middle value, not a rule for everyone.

guided.stem: Kavi says his friend must feel losses exactly twice as much as gains. What is wrong?
guided.hint: Is the figure for a group or for one person?

options.text: Twice is an average; people differ.
options.feedback: Right. The figure is pooled over studies, so one person can be above or below it.

options.text: Losses weigh less than gains.
options.feedback: On average losses weigh more. The point is that twice is an average, not a rule.

options.text: He is right; twice is a fixed rule for everyone.
options.feedback: Twice is pooled over many studies, and the figures varied, so one person can sit above or below it.

guided.stem: A new study finds losses weigh less than twice a same-size gain. Akash says this proves the pooled figure of about twice is wrong. Is he right?
guided.hint: Did every pooled study land on one number?

options.text: Yes; one study that differs breaks the average.
options.feedback: Figures varied from study to study, so one lower result does not break the pooled average.

options.text: No; figures vary, and twice is the average.
options.feedback: Right. Some studies found less and some more. About twice was the pooled average, so one lower study fits.

options.text: Yes; losses and gains weigh the same.
options.feedback: Less than twice is not the same as equal. Losses still weighed more than gains on average.

guided.stem: A shop owner in Jaipur is offered an even-chance deal: lose ₹1,000 or gain some sum. Using the average of about twice, what gain would make it feel roughly even to a typical owner?
guided.hint: How much heavier does a loss feel, on average?

options.text: About ₹1,000, as the odds are even.
options.feedback: Even odds do not make equal sums feel equal. On average, a loss weighed about twice a same-size gain.

options.text: About ₹4,000.
options.feedback: That doubles it twice. A loss weighed about twice a gain on average, so about ₹2,000 would balance it.

options.text: About ₹2,000.
options.feedback: Right. If a loss weighs about twice a gain on average, a gain near twice the loss roughly balances it. People differ, though.

steps.takeaway: On average a loss weighs about twice a gain; people differ.

concepts.title: Anchoring
concepts.hook: A random number can pull a later estimate: the first figure matters even when it has no link to the answer.
concepts.rule: An early number can pull a later guess toward it, even when it is random. Listing reasons the number might be wrong makes the pull smaller.

claims.text: A first number can pull a later estimate toward it, because people adjust away from it too little.
In one study, a random first number of 10 led to a median guess of 25, and a random 65 led to a median guess of 45. The median guess is the halfway value when guesses are ordered.
Experienced judges leaned toward a sentence demand even when they set it themselves by rolling dice.
In two studies, listing reasons why an anchor was wrong made its pull smaller.

items.stem: In a school quiz, Ritu is first asked if the Ganga is longer or shorter than 5,000 km, then asked its length. Her friend was first asked about 1,000 km. Who likely guesses a longer length?

options.text: Ritu, who heard the bigger number first.
options.feedback: Each starts from the number in the first question, so the bigger start tends to give the bigger guess.

options.text: Her friend, who heard the smaller number.
options.feedback: A smaller first number tends to pull the guess down, not up.

options.text: Both the same, since the river does not change.
options.feedback: The river is the same, but each guess starts from a different first number.

items.stem: Tejas guessed ₹700 for a bag. He began from a printed tag and came down only a little. So the tag most likely showed ___.

options.text: Far below ₹700, such as ₹200.
options.feedback: He came down from the tag, so it must have been higher than his guess.

options.text: The tag was ₹700, so his guess had to be ₹700.
options.feedback: An anchor can pull a guess without fixing it. He came down a little, so the tag was higher.

options.text: A bit above ₹700, such as ₹750.
options.feedback: People adjust too little from the first number, so a small move down points to a tag just above his guess.

items.stem: In one anchor study, people guessed a count of nations. After a random 10, the median guess was 25. What was it after a random 65?

options.text: About 45.
options.feedback: The high random number pulled the median guess up to about 45, short of 65.

options.text: About 65.
options.feedback: People adjusted away from 65, just not far enough, so the guess was lower.

options.text: About 25.
options.feedback: That was the guess after the low number. The high number pulled guesses up.

items.stem: Dr Rao has priced old cars in Mumbai for years. A buyer first mentions a random ₹9 lakh. Will his long experience keep his price free of that number?

options.text: Yes; experts are not swayed by chance numbers.
options.feedback: Studies of judges found expertise and experience did not reduce the pull.

options.text: Yes; a random first price cannot sway his guess.
options.feedback: Even a number known to be random can pull a guess. Experience did not remove that effect in the judge study.

options.text: No; even experts lean toward a random number.
options.feedback: Experienced judges still leaned toward a dice number, so expertise does not switch the pull off.

items.stem: A seller opens at ₹4,000 for a used cricket bat. Which buyer is least pulled by that number?

options.text: Neha, who first lists the bat's dents and worn grip.
options.feedback: Listing reasons the price is too high brings the other side to mind, which shrinks the pull.

options.text: Om, who treats the first price as the bat's fair value.
options.feedback: A first price is a starting point, not proof of fair value. Listing reasons against it can shrink its pull.

options.text: Ira, who assumes a random opening price cannot sway her.
options.feedback: Even a random first number can pull a later guess. Reasons against the price can reduce that pull.

items.stem: How would you sum up the list-reasons-against-it trick to a friend?

options.text: It removes the anchor's pull for good.
options.feedback: It reduced the pull, but did not remove it, so some pull stays.

options.text: It shrinks the anchor's pull, but some pull stays.
options.feedback: In studies the trick reduced the effect. It did not make the anchor vanish.

options.text: It works because a random first number has no pull.
options.feedback: A random number can still pull a guess. Listing reasons against it makes the pull smaller.

misconceptions.name: Random has no pull

misconceptions.name: Experts are immune
misconceptions.correction: Experienced judges still leaned toward a random number.

misconceptions.name: One trick erases it
misconceptions.correction: Listing reasons against an anchor shrinks its pull; it does not remove it.

misconceptions.name: An anchor fixes the answer
misconceptions.correction: A first number pulls a guess toward it, but the guess can differ from that number.

steps.title: A first number pulls your guess

hook.stem: A seller first says a kurta costs ₹2,000, then offers it for ₹1,200. Why does ₹1,200 seem cheap?

options.text: The ₹2,000 came first.
options.feedback: Right. The first price set the starting point, so ₹1,200 looks low next to it.

options.text: ₹1,200 is the usual kurta price.
options.feedback: Nothing here says what kurtas usually cost. The first number shaped the feel.

options.text: The seller is being generous.
options.feedback: The seller set the high first number. That is what makes ₹1,200 seem cheap.

steps.teach: The first number you see becomes a starting point, called an anchor. You adjust away from it, but not far enough, so your guess ends up near it.

parts: Rohit hears “50,000” on TV,
then guesses that 45,000 people
fit in the new stadium.
example.spot: Rohit hears “50,000” on TV,
example.feedback: He heard 50,000 first, and his guess stayed close to it.

guided.stem: Two shops sell the same shoes for ₹1,500. One tag says “was ₹2,500”; the other shows just ₹1,500. Why might the first feel like the better deal?
guided.hint: Ask which number the eye meets first on each tag.

options.text: The old price sets a high starting point.
options.feedback: Right. The ₹2,500 acts as an anchor, so ₹1,500 seems low beside it, though both shops charge the same.

options.text: The old price shows what they are worth.
options.feedback: The old price is a starting point, not proof of value. Both shops charge ₹1,500.

options.text: The tag shows the fair value is ₹2,500.
options.feedback: A first number is a starting point, not proof of fair value. It just makes ₹1,500 feel cheap beside it.

guided.stem: Pallavi hears a flat's rent was once ₹40,000. She knows that is too high, so she adjusts down before making her own guess. Where does her guess likely end?
guided.hint: How far do people move from a first number?

options.text: Still a bit high.
options.feedback: Right. People adjust away from an anchor, but not far enough, so her guess stays near it.

options.text: About right, since she knew to adjust.
options.feedback: Knowing to adjust is not enough. People move too little, so the guess stays pulled toward the first number.

options.text: A bit low, since she overcorrects.
options.feedback: The usual slip goes the other way. People adjust too little, so the guess stays on the high side.

guided.stem: At a job interview in Hyderabad, Naveen planned to ask for ₹4.5 lakh a year. The recruiter first says, "Freshers here often ask for ₹3 lakh." What is the likely pull?
guided.hint: Whose figure came first in the talk?

options.text: No pull, since he already had his own number.
options.feedback: A first number can still pull a later guess, even when you came in with your own plan.

options.text: His ask drifts down toward ₹3 lakh.
options.feedback: Right. The first number he heard becomes a start point, and people adjust away from it too little.

options.text: His ask goes up, to stand out.
options.feedback: Anchors pull guesses toward them. Hearing ₹3 lakh more likely drags his ask down, not up.

steps.takeaway: The first number you hear can steer your guess.

steps.title: Even a random number pulls

hook.stem: People spin a wheel to get a random number, say whether a fact is higher or lower, then guess it. Does the random number change their guess?

options.text: Yes, guesses drift toward it.
options.feedback: Right. Even a random number pulled the guesses toward it.

options.text: No, people ignore random numbers.
options.feedback: In the study, people did not ignore it. Their guesses moved toward it.

options.text: Just when the number is very large.
options.feedback: Both a small and a large random number pulled guesses toward them.

steps.teach: A random number can pull guesses, since people start from it. After a random 10, the median guess, the halfway value when guesses are ordered, was 25; after 65, 45.

visual.label: Median guess of a count of nations after a random number

example.ask: Tap where the dice number pulled them.
parts: Legal experts rolled dice to set a sentence demand,
then gave sentences that leaned toward the dice number,
though they knew it was chance.
example.spot: then gave sentences that leaned toward the dice number,
example.feedback: The dice number was pure chance, yet the experts' sentences leaned toward it.

guided.stem: Before a GK quiz, a screen asks if a tower is taller or shorter than a random 900 metres. Then Tara guesses 800 metres. Why so high?
guided.hint: Did the first number have any link to the tower?

options.text: The random figure pulled her guess up.
options.feedback: Yes. It had no link to the tower, yet it pulled her guess.

options.text: The tower must be close to 900 metres.
options.feedback: The 900 was random, with no link to the tower. It pulled her guess toward it all the same.

options.text: Random numbers have no effect.
options.feedback: In studies, random numbers still pulled guesses toward them.

guided.stem: In a wheel test, people who got a high random number gave a median guess well below it, yet above what a low-number group guessed. What does this show?
guided.hint: Compare each guess with its wheel number and with the other group.

options.text: The anchor fixed each guess at its own value.
options.feedback: The median guess was well below the high number, so it was not fixed there. It was only pulled toward it.

options.text: The random number had no real pull.
options.feedback: The high group guessed higher than the low group, so the random number did pull their guesses.

options.text: They adjusted, but too little.
options.feedback: Right. Each group moved away from its random start, but too little, so the groups stayed apart.

guided.stem: At a charity auction in Kolkata, the host spins a wheel "just for fun" before bidding on a painting. It lands on ₹8,000. What is likely to happen to the bids?
guided.hint: What do people start from when they are unsure?

options.text: Bids lean toward ₹8,000.
options.feedback: Right. Even a number known to be random can become a start point, so bids drift toward it.

options.text: Bids ignore it.
options.feedback: Knowing a number is random does not stop its pull. Guesses after a random number still leaned toward it.

options.text: Bids drop below it.
options.feedback: Anchors pull toward themselves. A random ₹8,000 more likely draws bids toward it, not away.

steps.takeaway: Even a made-up number can tug your guess toward it.

steps.title: Argue against the anchor

hook.stem: A shop shows a huge “was” price. Which trick could weaken its pull on you?

options.text: List reasons that price might be wrong.
options.feedback: Right. Thinking of reasons against the first number shrank its pull in two studies.

options.text: Stare at the price for longer.
options.feedback: Looking longer keeps the number in mind. Arguing against it helps more.

options.text: Trust it, since shops know prices.
options.feedback: The shop chose that number. Trusting it keeps the pull strong.

steps.teach: Listing reasons why a first number might be wrong makes its pull smaller, because it brings the other side to mind. It weakens the anchor; it does not erase it.

nodes: List why it may be wrong

example.ask: Tap the step that weakens the pull.
parts: A car seller names ₹8 lakh,
so Nisha lists three reasons the car is worth less,
then makes her own offer.
example.spot: so Nisha lists three reasons the car is worth less,
example.feedback: Listing reasons against ₹8 lakh brings the other side to mind, which shrinks its pull.

guided.stem: Meena plans to list reasons against a seller’s first price before she bargains. What can she expect?
guided.hint: Think about what the two studies found.

options.text: A smaller pull, though some stays.
options.feedback: Right. Listing reasons brings the other side to mind, which shrinks the pull without erasing it.

options.text: No change; an anchor cannot be weakened.
options.feedback: Listing reasons did weaken the pull in two studies, so it does help.

options.text: The pull will be wiped out for good.
options.feedback: It shrinks the pull, but in the studies some of it stayed.

guided.stem: Vani lists three reasons a dealer's ₹6 lakh ask is too high. She still offers ₹5.5 lakh, fairly close to it. Did the trick fail?
guided.hint: Recall what the two studies found about the size of the effect.

options.text: Yes; if it had worked, she could have ignored ₹6 lakh fully.
options.feedback: The trick weakens an anchor; it does not erase it. Some leftover pull is what the studies would expect.

options.text: Not really; it weakens the pull, so some stays.
options.feedback: Right. Listing reasons against an anchor shrinks its pull. Some pull can remain, so a close offer does not mean failure.

options.text: Yes; listing reasons just adds to the pull.
options.feedback: Listing reasons against the number made its pull smaller in two studies, not bigger.

guided.stem: A client tells Shreya, a project lead in Gurugram, "This app should take two weeks." Before giving her own time estimate, what is most likely to weaken that number's pull?
guided.hint: Which step brings the other side to mind?

options.text: Waiting a day so the number fades.
options.feedback: Waiting was not what the studies tested. Listing reasons against the number is what made its pull smaller.

options.text: Averaging the client's number with her own.
options.feedback: Averaging keeps the client's number in the sum, so its pull stays. Listing reasons against it is what helped.

options.text: Listing reasons against two weeks.
options.feedback: Right. Listing reasons against a first number brings the other side to mind, so its pull shrinks.

steps.takeaway: Arguing against the first number weakens its pull.

concepts.title: Confirmation bias
concepts.hook: In Wason's card task, most people turned a card that could prove the rule right and skipped the one that could prove it wrong.
concepts.rule: Confirmation bias is a pull to seek or notice clues that fit a belief. A fair test also looks for clues that could show the belief is wrong.

claims.text: People tend to focus on information that fits what they already believe and pass over what does not.
A rule of the form 'if p then q' is tested properly by checking the cases that could prove it false.
In Wason's number puzzle, only 6 of 29 people found the rule without first naming a wrong one, since cases that fit a guess can fit other rules too.
On the classic card puzzle, only around 1 in 5 people usually pick the cards that could prove the rule wrong.

items.stem: Kabir is sure the hostel mess food got worse this term. Which meals will he talk about most?

options.text: A fair mix of good and bad meals.
options.feedback: A fair mix would need him to count both sides, which a strong belief makes hard.

options.text: He will give good and bad meals the same weight.
options.feedback: People tend to notice evidence that fits their view. Kabir is more likely to discuss this term's bad meals.

options.text: The bad meals that fit his view.
options.feedback: Meals that fit his belief stand out to him, so those are the ones he brings up.

items.stem: Match each remembered clue to the belief behind it.

options.text: Recalls the day she gave extra homework
options.feedback: This clue fits a belief that the teacher is strict.

options.text: Thinks the new teacher is strict
options.feedback: A strict-teacher belief makes the extra homework day stand out.

options.text: Remembers the defeat at their own ground
options.feedback: This clue fits a belief that the team does badly at home.

options.text: Thinks his team plays badly at home
options.feedback: This belief makes the defeat at their own ground stick in memory.

options.text: Remembers the wet day in Goa
options.feedback: This clue fits a belief that rain follows him on trips.

options.text: Thinks rain follows him on trips
options.feedback: This belief makes the wet holiday stand out more than the dry ones.

items.stem: In Wason's number test, about what percent of people found the rule without first naming a wrong one?

options.text: About 21%.
options.feedback: Right. Only 6 of 29 found it without a wrong guess first, about one in five.

options.text: About 50%.
options.feedback: Far fewer than half managed it. Only 6 of 29 found the rule without a wrong guess first.

options.text: About 79%.
options.feedback: That is the share who named a wrong rule first. Only about 21% found it straight away.

items.stem: Sameer, a college student, thinks his UPI app is slow every evening. He notes only slow evening payments and never tries one in the morning to compare. What is going wrong?

options.text: He keeps fitting cases and runs no test that could say no.
options.feedback: He counts only clues that fit and skips the test that could show his idea is wrong.

options.text: He tests fairly, since he took notes.
options.feedback: Notes help only if they cover both sides. His cover only the slow evenings.

options.text: His slow payments prove the app is slow each evening.
options.feedback: Fitting cases do not settle the claim. He needs a case that could show his view is wrong.

items.stem: Kavya runs a shop and thinks her newspaper ads bring in the crowds. To test it, she plans to count crowds only in weeks with an ad. What is she missing?

options.text: A week with no ad could show her wrong.
options.feedback: Right. Crowds in ad weeks fit many reasons. A week without an ad is the test that could say no.

options.text: No gap; ad weeks are the right test.
options.feedback: Ad weeks can only agree with her. A test needs a case that could prove the idea wrong.

options.text: She should count her busiest weeks instead.
options.feedback: Best weeks fit her belief even more. A strong test looks for a case that could break it.

items.stem: Nidhi says trains on her line are usually late. Her friend finds one train that came on time and calls her claim broken. Why is the friend off here?

options.text: On-time trains do not count as evidence.
options.feedback: They do count. One just is not enough against a claim that says usually.

options.text: Exceptions cannot test any kind of claim.
options.feedback: Exceptions are strong tests for always claims. This claim only says usually.

options.text: One exception cannot break a usually claim.
options.feedback: A single exception breaks a claim that says always. A claim that says usually allows a few.

misconceptions.name: One match proves it
misconceptions.correction: One fitting case may fit more than one idea.

misconceptions.correction: A case against an idea can test it well.

hook.stem: Mohit thinks his lucky pen helps in exams. Which exams does he recall best?

steps.title: Fitting cases prove little

hook.stem: A friend's secret rule fits 2, 4, 8. You test 16, 32 and she says it fits. Is the rule surely doubling?

options.text: No; many rules fit those numbers.
options.feedback: Right. Any rising numbers fit too, so fitting cases cannot pin the rule down.

options.text: Yes; it fit twice in a row.
options.feedback: Both tests fit doubling, but they also fit many other rules.

options.text: Yes, if the numbers are even.
options.feedback: Even numbers fit lots of rules. Fitting cases still prove little.

steps.teach: Cases that fit your guess can fit other rules too, so they prove little. In one puzzle, just 6 of 29 people found the rule without a wrong guess first.

Ali tries 10, 20, 30,

options.feedback: Right. Cases that fit her idea also fit another cause, summer heat, so they prove little on their own.

options.text: A few weeks are too few, so more weeks could settle it.
options.feedback: More summer weeks would not help. Each would still fit both the sign and the heat.

options.text: Sales rises cannot be measured.
options.feedback: Sales can be counted. The problem is that the rise fits more than one cause.

steps.takeaway: Cases that fit a guess can fit other rules too.

steps.title: Hunt for the case that breaks it

hook.stem: A friend says every crow is black. What would test that claim best?

options.text: Looking for a crow that is not black.
options.feedback: Right. One crow of another colour would break the claim. That is a strong test.

options.text: Counting more black crows.
options.feedback: Each black crow fits, but it cannot show the claim is wrong. A strong test looks for one that breaks it.

options.text: Asking friends if they agree.
options.feedback: Agreement is not a test. A crow of another colour would be.

steps.teach: A strong test looks for a case that could prove the idea wrong, since fitting cases prove little. One clear exception can break an always claim.

right.title: Strong test
lines: Look for a case that breaks it

example.ask: Tap the test that could break his idea.
parts: To test his idea that the 8 o’clock bus is always late,
Farhan skips counting the late days
and looks for a day it came on time.
example.spot: and looks for a day it came on time.
example.feedback: One on-time day would break “always late,” so it is a strong test.

guided.stem: Dev says phones that cost more always have better cameras. Which phone could prove him wrong?

options.text: A costly phone with a weak camera.
options.feedback: Yes. One such phone would break his claim.

options.text: A parcel with no red sticker.

options.text: A parcel not marked Express.

guided.stem: Mahesh, a farmer in Punjab, believes his field gives more grain when he sows after the first rain. Which record would test this idea best?
guided.hint: Which record could prove him wrong?

options.text: More good seasons sown after the first rain.
options.feedback: Good seasons fit his idea, but fitting cases prove little. The test is a case that could break it.

options.text: His neighbour's view on the best time to sow.
options.feedback: A view is not a test. The strong test is a case that could prove his idea wrong.

options.text: Rain-sown seasons with a poor crop.
options.feedback: Right. A strong test looks for cases that could break the idea. Poor seasons after rain would do that.

steps.takeaway: To test an idea, look for the case that could break it.

concepts.title: Social proof
concepts.hook: In Asch's line test, a group giving a plainly wrong answer still pulled some people away from what they could see.
concepts.rule: When we are unsure, a crowd's choice can act as a clue and pull our own. Even when we are sure, a group can pull us to fit in. Group agreement is not proof.

claims.text: In Asch's line test, people went along with a wrong group in 36.8% of answers, against under 1% of mistakes when alone. The group was wrong on 12 of each 18 trials.
When people are unsure, they may follow a group because they believe it has the right information.
A group can agree on a wrong answer, so agreement alone is a clue, not proof.
People differed a lot: about a quarter of Asch's subjects never went along with the wrong group.
In Asch's test the right answer was plain, so people who went along mostly did it to fit in and avoid ridicule; some decided they must be wrong.

items.stem: Two chai stalls stand side by side outside the college. One has a long queue; the other is empty. Which one will a new student likely pick?

options.text: The one with the queue.
options.feedback: A queue tells her many others chose it, so she takes it as a sign of good chai.

options.text: The empty one, since there is no wait for chai.
options.feedback: No wait is a plus, but the crowd at the other stall works as a strong clue.

options.text: Neither; queues put people off.
options.feedback: A queue can put some off, but more often it reads as a sign the stall is good.

items.stem: A new snack stall's owner asks friends to stand in a queue on opening day. What is she counting on?

options.text: Passers-by reading the queue as a sign the food is good.
options.feedback: Right. Many people choosing something is taken as a clue it is good, so a queue draws more people in.

options.text: Her friends buying most of the food.
options.feedback: A few friends cannot buy much. The queue is there to be seen, as a sign that others chose it.

options.text: A queue that puts other buyers off.
options.feedback: A queue tends to pull people in, because many others choosing a stall reads as a sign it is good.

items.stem: In Asch's line test, when the group gave a plainly wrong answer, about what percent of answers went along with it?

options.text: About 37%.
options.feedback: Right. About a third of answers went along with the wrong group, though about a quarter of people never did.

options.text: About 5%.
options.feedback: Far more went along than that. About a third of answers followed the group's wrong call.

options.text: About 95%.
options.feedback: Most answers stayed right. About a third went along, and about a quarter of people never gave in.

items.stem: During a school quiz, all four students before Ira give a clearly wrong answer. Ira gives the right one. Does this go against the Asch finding?

options.text: Yes; the finding is that everyone goes along.
options.feedback: The finding was about a third of answers, so most answers stayed right, just as Ira’s did.

options.text: No; people went along in only about a third of answers.
options.feedback: Going along in about a third of answers leaves most answers right, so Ira staying right fits the finding.

options.text: Yes; school quizzes are far too easy for the effect to show.
options.feedback: Asch's lines were easy too. The effect is about some answers, not everyone.

items.stem: Match each crowd claim to a fresh check that settles it.

options.text: Whole hostel says the mess is shut on Sunday
options.feedback: Many voices agree, but the notice board can settle it.

options.text: Read the notice board
options.feedback: The board gives the facts, apart from what the hostel is saying.

options.text: Fifty forwards claim a holiday tomorrow
options.feedback: Many forwards may all come from one message, so check the source.

options.text: Look at the school's official site
options.feedback: The school's own site is the place to check if the holiday is real.

options.text: A huge crowd cheers that the batter is out
options.feedback: Loud cheers show what fans believe, not what happened.

options.text: Watch the third umpire's replay
options.feedback: The replay is a fresh check that does not depend on the crowd.

items.stem: A video has a crore likes, so Dhruv says its health tip must be true. What is not quite right?

options.text: Likes show agreement, not that the tip is right.
options.feedback: Many people agreeing is a clue, not proof. The tip still needs a fresh check.

options.text: A crore people cannot be wrong together.
options.feedback: A big group can agree on a wrong answer, as Asch's test showed.

options.text: Real likes prove the health tip is right.
options.feedback: Even genuine agreement is a clue, not proof. The tip does not become true because many people liked it.

steps.title: A crowd’s choice is a clue

hook.stem: In class, everyone around you raises a hand for answer B. You thought A. What do you feel pulled to do?

options.text: Switch to B.
options.feedback: Right. When many people pick one answer, it pulls on our own choice.

options.text: Feel more sure of A.
options.feedback: Usually the pull goes the other way, toward the group’s answer.

options.text: No pull, since others do not matter.
options.feedback: Others do matter. A group answer can pull our own.

steps.teach: When we are unsure and many people pick something, we take it as a sign it is right, so we lean their way. This pull is social proof.

options.text: He copies others as a habit, whatever the setting.
options.feedback: Anyone can lean on a crowd when unsure. It is not a fixed copycat trait; here he simply does not know.

options.text: Their choice tells him where it goes.
options.feedback: Right. When unsure, we take what many people do as a clue to what is right, so he copies them.

options.text: He fears being told off by the boss on day one.
options.feedback: Nothing points to fear here. He is unsure, so he treats the crowd's choice as useful information.

steps.takeaway: What a crowd picks can pull your own pick.

steps.title: Even a wrong crowd can pull

hook.stem: In a test, a group gives a plainly wrong answer about line lengths. How often did the one real person go along?

options.text: Wanting to fit in with the class.
options.feedback: Right. In Asch’s test the answer was plain, so most who went along did it to fit in. A quarter never gave in.

options.text: No pull; people do not go along when an answer is plain.
options.feedback: In Asch’s test the answer was plain, yet people went along in about a third of answers, mostly to fit in.

options.text: A whole class is hardly ever wrong.
options.feedback: A group can be plainly wrong, as in Asch’s test. She went along to fit in, not because they were right.

guided.stem: In Asch's line test, mistakes went from under 1% when people were alone to about a third of answers with a wrong group. What does that jump show?

options.text: The lines were hard to judge for most people.
options.feedback: Alone, people made mistakes under 1% of the time, so the lines were easy. The group made the difference.

guided.hint: In Asch's test, was the right answer hard to see?

options.text: Not wanting to stand out from the group.
options.feedback: Right. In Asch's test the answer was plain, so most who went along did it to fit in.

options.text: She doubts her own eyes.

steps.title: Agreement is not proof

hook.stem: Thirty classmates forward the same message saying the exam is moved. Does that make it true?

options.text: No, they may all be sharing one message.
options.feedback: Right. Many people agreeing is not a fresh check of the fact.

options.text: Yes, so many people cannot be wrong.
options.feedback: A group can share one mistake. In Asch’s test, groups agreed on a wrong answer.

options.text: Yes, if they are close friends.
options.feedback: Friends can share a mistake too. Agreement is not proof.

steps.teach: A crowd can agree on a wrong answer, so many people saying the same thing is a clue, not proof. The facts still need their own check.

when Sid checks the menu,
it says Thursday.

example.feedback: Everyone agreed, yet the menu was the real check, and it showed they were wrong.

options.text: Only that they agree.
options.feedback: Yes. Agreement is not a check. The working would be.

options.text: That 42 is right, since five people agree.
options.feedback: Not yet. A group can agree on a wrong answer, so agreement is a clue, not proof.

options.text: That 42 is checked, since they agree.

options.text: About as much as one report.
options.feedback: Right. Ten people passing on one source is still one source. Agreement is a clue, and this one is thin.

options.text: Full proof, since ten people agree.
options.feedback: A crowd can agree on a wrong answer. Agreement is a clue, so the facts still need a check.

guided.stem: Hundreds of people in a WhatsApp group say a new coin will soon double in price. What does that agreement tell Abhay by itself?
guided.hint: Has anyone checked the facts?

options.text: That it is likely true.
options.feedback: A crowd can agree on a wrong answer. Numbers alone do not make a claim true.

options.text: That it is checked, since a big group would spot errors.

options.text: That many people in the group say so.

steps.takeaway: Many people agreeing is a clue, not proof.

concepts.title: The planning fallacy
concepts.hook: In a study, people's guesses for their own tasks ran too short. When they linked past tasks to the new plan, the gap went away.
concepts.rule: The planning fallacy is a tilt toward a short time guess for our own task. Looking at past tasks and missed steps can give a better time guess.

claims.text: People's guesses of how long their own tasks would take were too short, for school tasks and other tasks alike.
In one study, asking people to link past tasks to a new plan removed the too-short bias.
When people plan, they think about how the task will go and pay little heed to how past tasks went.
People guessing how long someone else's task would take guessed long, not short, and used past cases more.
People tended to put their past late finishes down to outside, one-off causes.

items.stem: Your college fest team guesses the stage decor will take one afternoon. What is most likely?

options.text: It finishes early, as teams plan well together.
options.feedback: Teams are planning their own task, so their guess tends to run short too.

options.text: It runs past the afternoon.
options.feedback: Guesses for our own tasks tend to run short, so the decor will likely take longer.

options.text: It takes the one afternoon they guessed.
options.feedback: That is possible, but guesses for our own tasks tend to fall short.

items.stem: Arya guesses how long her hostel roommate's room clean-up will take, and how long her own will take. Which guess is more likely to run short?

options.text: Her guess for her roommate's room.
options.feedback: When people guess for others, they tend to guess long and lean on past cases.

options.text: Both equally, since the rooms are alike.
options.feedback: The rooms match, but people guess differently for their own task and a friend's.

options.text: Her guess for her own room.
options.feedback: People tend to guess short for their own tasks, but not for someone else's.

options.feedback: Guesses for our own tasks tend to fall short, so start by doubting the first one.

options.text: List the steps the smooth picture leaves out.
options.feedback: A smooth picture skips delays and extra steps, so name them.

options.text: Add time for each of those steps.
options.feedback: Each hidden step takes time, so the guess grows to fit them.

options.text: Make the final time guess from that full list.
options.feedback: A guess built on the full list is less likely to run short.

items.stem: Neha's model took 3 hours, not the 1 she planned. Working back, her plan most likely left out ___.

options.text: no step, since a smooth path is the normal one
options.feedback: A smooth plan can miss snags and side jobs. Those extra steps help explain the longer finish.

options.text: No step; she just worked slowly that day.
options.feedback: Slow work is possible, but plans usually miss delays and extra steps.

options.text: Snags and side jobs along the way.
options.feedback: A smooth picture leaves out delays and extra steps, so they are the likely gap.

items.stem: Past club posters took 5, 6 and 7 hours. The plan for a new one says 2 hours. What is a better estimate?

options.text: About 6 hours.
options.feedback: Past tasks are a good guide, and the middle of 5, 6 and 7 is 6.

options.text: About 2 hours.

options.text: About 10 hours.
options.feedback: That is longer than any past poster took. The past points to about 6.

options.text: Printer jams take no real time, so they can safely be left out.
options.feedback: Jams do take time. The trouble is treating them as if they will not happen again.

options.text: Calling each delay a fluke keeps it out of the next plan.
options.feedback: If every past delay is a one-off, the next plan leaves delays out and runs short again.

options.text: The printer jam was a fluke, so past delays add no time.
options.feedback: Dismissing past delays keeps them out of the next plan. Some delay can still make the guess short.

guided.stem: Arjun, a junior engineer in Ahmedabad, plans a report in two steps: write, then send. Past reports all needed his manager's sign-off, which took days. What kind of slip is this?
guided.hint: What did earlier reports show?

options.text: Leaving out a step that past tasks showed.
options.feedback: Right. When we plan, we picture the smooth path and pay little heed to how past tasks went.

options.text: Bad luck each time.
options.feedback: Every past report needed it, so it is not a fluke. Calling delays one-offs keeps guesses short.

options.text: Too much detail.
options.feedback: His plan had too little detail, not too much. It left out a step past tasks showed.

steps.title: Past tasks give a better guess

hook.stem: Your last three lab reports took 2, 3 and 4 hours. A new one is due. What is a fair time guess?

options.text: About 3 hours.
options.feedback: Right. Your past reports are a real guide, and they took about 3 hours.

options.text: About 1 hour, if it goes well.
options.feedback: That pictures a smooth path. Past reports took 2 to 4 hours.

options.text: There is no way to guess.
options.feedback: There is. Past reports took 2 to 4 hours, so about 3 is fair.

steps.teach: How long similar tasks really took is a good guide, so link them to the new plan. In one study, doing this removed the too-short guesses.

options.text: The 2 hours it took before.
options.feedback: Right. Past setups show the real time, delays and all.

options.text: 30 minutes; last time’s delays were bad luck.

options.text: The time printed on the recipe.
options.feedback: A recipe time shows how it should go. Her own past cakes show how it really went for her.

options.text: How long her last few cakes took.
options.feedback: Right. How long similar tasks really took is a good guide. Linking past tasks to the plan removed short guesses.

options.text: How long a TV chef took on a show.

guided.stem: Karan moves to a new Delhi flat. A map app says his office trip takes 25 minutes. A friend on the same road says it usually takes her 50. What gives the better guess?
guided.hint: Which number is based on what happened before?

options.text: Trust the app's figure.
options.feedback: The app shows a smooth trip. Her real trips on that road are the better guide.

options.text: Splitting the two, as both are guesses.

concepts.title: Sleep and memory
concepts.hook: New learning can become more stable during sleep, even without another round of practice.
concepts.rule: Sleep supports the later strengthening and organising of some new memories; it does not replace learning in the first place.

claims.text: Sleep after learning reduced forgetting, compared with the same length of time awake.
A brief spell of quiet rest while awake after learning helped memory more than spending that time on other tasks.
After you learn, a new memory is firmed up over time. This is called consolidation.
In a pilot of 8 people with a mean age of 59, word-pair recall after 12 hours was about 20.4 with sleep and 12.6 awake.
Across 177 papers, people who slept after learning recalled more than people who stayed awake for the same time.

items.stem: A week later, Tanu still recalls a poem easily. Working back, what came first?

options.text: She learned it, then it firmed up over time.
options.feedback: You learn it first, and then the memory firms up over time.

options.text: She learned it and it became firm at once.
options.feedback: A new memory gets firm over time, after you learn it. So she learned it first, then it set.

options.text: She heard it once, played aloud while she slept.
options.feedback: Sleep helps store what was learned awake. It does not supply a new poem.

items.stem: In exam week, Yusuf crams new formulas until 3 a.m. and leaves for the exam at 7. What does consolidation suggest?

options.text: Cramming late at night makes new memories firmer by morning.
options.feedback: Late cramming leaves little time and sleep for new memories to firm up.

options.text: His new formulas have had little time to firm up.
options.feedback: Firming up takes time after learning, and he left very little of it.

options.text: Firming up is done the moment he reads.
options.feedback: The memory firms up over time after you learn, not at the very moment you read.

items.stem: In a small sleep pilot, recall after sleep was about 60% higher than after the same hours awake. If that gap held in a chemistry class and the awake group recalled 10 new terms, about how many might the sleepers recall?

options.text: About 16 terms.
options.feedback: Right. 60% more than 10 is 6 more, so about 16, if the pilot's gap held for chemistry terms.

options.text: About 10 terms.
options.feedback: That leaves out the gap. In the pilot, sleepers recalled about 60% more than people who stayed awake.

options.text: About 70 terms.
options.feedback: That adds 60 terms, not 60%. Six tenths of 10 is 6, so about 16 terms.

items.stem: Before a college viva, Imran thinks sleep is wasted time and stays up to keep his notes fresh. What does the research suggest?

options.text: Staying awake keeps new memories fresher.
options.feedback: Studies found more forgetting after time awake than after sleep.

options.text: Sleep after study tends to cut forgetting.
options.feedback: Sleep after study cut forgetting, compared with the same hours spent awake.

options.text: Sleep just pauses the brain for the night.
options.feedback: The sleeping brain helps firm up new memories, so it is not a mere pause.

items.stem: Match each case to what it does for memory.

options.text: A night of sleep after study
options.feedback: Sleep after you learn cuts down on how much you forget.

options.text: Less forgetting the next day
options.feedback: This is what sleep after learning tends to give.

options.text: Ten quiet minutes, eyes shut
options.feedback: Quiet rest after learning helped memory more than busy tasks.

options.text: Can help a new memory settle
options.feedback: This matches a short spell of quiet rest after learning.

options.text: Skipping the lesson itself
options.feedback: With no learning, there is no new memory at all.

options.text: Nothing to firm up later
options.feedback: Consolidation needs a memory to work on, so a skipped lesson gives none.

items.stem: How would you describe a study break that helps memory to a friend?

options.text: Jump straight into reels for a while to relax the mind.
options.feedback: Reels are a busy task. Quiet rest with nothing to do is what helped.

options.text: Breaks undo what you just learned.
options.feedback: Quiet breaks after learning helped memory in studies, so they do not undo it.

options.text: Rest quietly a few minutes before the next task.
options.feedback: Quiet rest after learning helped memory more than jumping into other tasks.

misconceptions.name: Sleep is only a pause
misconceptions.correction: The brain can process recent learning during sleep.

misconceptions.name: Sleep teaches unseen material
misconceptions.correction: Sleep can help store what was learned, but it does not supply an unread lesson.

misconceptions.name: Staying up beats sleeping after study
misconceptions.correction: Sleep after learning reduced forgetting compared with the same length of time awake.

misconceptions.name: Memories firm up at once
misconceptions.correction: A new memory firms up over time after learning.

misconceptions.name: Busy breaks aid memory
misconceptions.correction: Quiet rest after learning helped memory more than spending that time on other tasks.
