steps.title: Learn first, then it firms up

hook.stem: Rohan sleeps with his textbook under his pillow but never opens it. Will he remember the chapter?

options.text: No, he never learned it.
options.feedback: Right. Sleep can firm up a memory, but only one he has already learned.

options.text: Yes, sleep will add it.
options.feedback: Sleep helps store what was learned. It cannot add a chapter he never read.

options.text: Yes, if he sleeps long enough.
options.feedback: No amount of sleep can store a chapter he never opened.

steps.teach: You learn first, and then the new memory firms up over time. That later step is called consolidation, so sleep cannot store a lesson you never took in.

parts: Divya reads her notes on the Mughals carefully,
and a week later
the dates still come back easily.
example.spot: Divya reads her notes on the Mughals carefully,
example.feedback: Reading carefully is the learning step. Only after it can the memory firm up and last.

guided.stem: Faisal learns ten new Hindi words today. Over the next days the words feel steadier. What is that later step called?
guided.hint: It is the firming up after learning.

options.text: Consolidation.
options.feedback: Yes. Consolidation is the firming up of a memory after learning.

options.text: Learning.
options.feedback: Learning came first, today. The later firming up is consolidation.

options.text: Forgetting.
options.feedback: The words are getting steadier, not fading. That is consolidation.

guided.stem: For sleep to help a new memory, which has to happen first?
guided.hint: What does consolidation need to work on?

options.text: Taking in the material while awake.
options.feedback: Right. You learn first, and then the memory firms up over time. Sleep cannot store a lesson never taken in.

options.text: Sleeping long enough that night.
options.feedback: Sleep can help firm up what was learned, but something has to be learned first.

options.text: Hearing the lesson play during sleep.
options.feedback: Consolidation works on what you already took in. It does not supply an unread lesson.

guided.stem: On her first day at a bank in Mysuru, Anjali watches the cash machine steps once, takes no notes and does not try them. Her friend says a good night's sleep will lock them in. What is the flaw?
guided.hint: What does sleep need to work with?

options.text: None; sleep can lock in anything seen that day.
options.feedback: Sleep can help store what was learned, but it cannot supply what was never taken in.

options.text: Little was learned, so little can firm up.
options.feedback: Right. Consolidation firms up what you took in. If the steps were barely learned, there is little to firm up.

options.text: Memories firm up at once.
options.feedback: A new memory firms up over time after learning, not at once.

steps.takeaway: Learn first; the memory firms up later.

steps.title: Sleep helps memories last

hook.stem: Two groups learn word pairs. One sleeps, the other stays awake for the same hours. Which group recalls more later?

options.text: The group that slept.
options.feedback: Right. In many studies, sleep after learning helps later recall.

options.text: The group that stayed awake.
options.feedback: Staying awake did not help more. In studies, sleep after learning helped recall.

options.text: Both recall the same.
options.feedback: In many studies, the sleep group recalled more.

steps.teach: Sleep after learning cuts forgetting, compared with the same hours awake. That is because the sleeping brain helps firm up new memories.

example.ask: Tap what came between learning and morning.
parts: Gautam learns the names of ten ragas in the evening,
sleeps,
and the next morning he still recalls most of them.
example.spot: sleeps,
example.feedback: Sleep after learning can cut how much of new facts and names is forgotten.

guided.stem: Sara learns a list of capitals at night, then sleeps. Ali learns it in the morning and stays awake all day. Who may recall more after the same gap?
guided.hint: Who slept after learning?

options.text: Sara.
options.feedback: Yes. Sleep after learning can help later recall. A big review found a moderate gain for facts and words.

options.text: Ali.
options.feedback: Ali stayed awake. In studies, sleep after learning tended to help recall more.

options.text: Both the same, since sleep is just a pause.
options.feedback: Sleep is not just a pause. The sleeping brain helps firm up new memories, so Sara may recall more.

guided.stem: Kunal says sleep after study just pauses the brain, so it cannot help memory more than lying awake for the same hours. What do the studies suggest?
guided.hint: What did the two groups in the studies show?

options.text: He is right; sleep is just a pause.
options.feedback: Sleep is more than a pause. The sleeping brain helps firm up new memories.

options.text: Lying awake helps more, as the brain keeps working.
options.feedback: It ran the other way. Sleep after learning reduced forgetting compared with the same time awake.

options.text: Sleep cut forgetting more than the same time awake.
options.feedback: Right. People who slept after learning forgot less than people awake for the same length of time.

guided.stem: Rohan, a tabla student, learns a new rhythm at his evening class. Which plan gives it the best chance of sticking by tomorrow's class?
guided.hint: What did the sleep studies compare?

options.text: Sleeping at his usual time.
options.feedback: Right. Sleep after learning cut forgetting compared with the same hours awake.

options.text: Staying up late to replay it again and again.
options.feedback: More time awake is not better here. Sleep after learning reduced forgetting compared with staying up.

options.text: Watching films late into the night to rest.
options.feedback: A night awake is not rest for memory. Sleep after learning helped people forget less.

steps.takeaway: Sleep after learning helps new memories stick.

steps.title: Quiet rest helps too

hook.stem: After a lesson, Jaya sits quietly for ten minutes with her eyes closed. Can that help her memory?

options.text: Yes, quiet rest can help.
options.feedback: Right. A short spell of quiet rest after learning helped memory in studies.

options.text: No, sleep is the one thing that helps.
options.feedback: Sleep helps, but quiet rest while awake helped memory too.

options.text: No, it is a waste of time.
options.feedback: Studies found that quiet rest after learning helped memory.

steps.teach: Sleep is not the only help. A few minutes of quiet, wakeful rest after learning helped memory more than other tasks did, so a calm break counts.

parts: After learning a list of new biology terms,
Lakshmi sits quietly for a few minutes,
and later she recalls the terms well.
example.spot: Lakshmi sits quietly for a few minutes,
example.feedback: Quiet rest after learning can help new memories firm up.

guided.stem: Between two exams, Rhea naps for a bit, then rests with her eyes closed. Which can help her new memories?
guided.hint: Can a wakeful break help as well?

options.text: Both the nap and the quiet rest.
options.feedback: Yes. Sleep can help, and quiet waking rest can help too.

options.text: Just the nap.
options.feedback: The nap can help, and so can quiet waking rest.

options.text: Neither.
options.feedback: Both can help new memories firm up.

guided.stem: After a coding lesson, Sid has a short break. Which use of it is most likely to help him recall the lesson later?
guided.hint: Which break gives the brain the least new input?

options.text: Playing a fast game on his phone.
options.feedback: A busy task fills the break. Quiet rest helped memory more than spending the time on other tasks.

options.text: Sitting quietly with his eyes closed.
options.feedback: Right. A spell of quiet, wakeful rest after learning helped memory more than other tasks.

options.text: Starting the next new lesson at once.
options.feedback: New work right away is another task. Quiet rest helped memory more than other tasks did.

guided.stem: After a training session on new billing software at her office in Coimbatore, Malini has a gap before her shift. What use of it best fits the rest finding?
guided.hint: Which choice adds the least?

options.text: Scrolling the news to relax.
options.feedback: Scrolling is still a task that brings new input. Quiet rest helped memory more than other tasks.

options.text: Answering emails, since any break helps the same.
options.feedback: Not every break is equal. Quiet rest helped memory more than doing other tasks.

options.text: Sitting calmly and letting her mind rest.
options.feedback: Right. A brief spell of quiet rest after learning helped memory more than spending that time on other tasks.

steps.takeaway: Sleep helps memory, and so can quiet rest while awake.

concepts.title: Variable rewards
concepts.hook: A surprise good post can make the next swipe tempting, even after several dull ones.
concepts.rule: When rewards arrive after an unknown number of tries, the next try can seem worth making. This helps explain repeated checking, though apps and people have other reasons too.

claims.text: On a variable schedule, people keep responding at a high, steady rate because they never know when the next reward is coming, and the habit is slow to fade.
Apps use several features besides surprise rewards, such as endless scrolling and read ticks that turn blue, which can stretch the time people spend on them.
On a variable schedule, the number of tries needed for a reward keeps changing, so you cannot tell which try will bring it.
A reward after every try is the quickest way to teach a new behaviour.
In over a million posts, people spaced their posts in a way that collected more likes, and people use social media for many motives.

items.stem: Which of these is a variable reward?

options.text: A lucky draw on UPI payments, won at random.
options.feedback: You cannot tell which payment will win, so the reward is variable.

options.text: Cashback of ₹10 on every fifth payment you make.
options.feedback: Every fifth payment is a set count, so you know when it comes. That is fixed.

options.text: A prize after ten payments, then ten more.
options.feedback: That gap is fixed. With variable rewards, the number of tries before a prize changes.

items.stem: Saina is teaching her younger brother to put his shoes on the rack. Why might she praise him each time at first, not now and then?

options.text: Uneven, now-and-then praise teaches a brand new act fastest.
options.feedback: Uneven rewards keep an act going. For teaching it first, a reward each time is quicker.

options.text: A reward on each try teaches a new act fastest.
options.feedback: Rewarding every time is the quickest way to teach a new behaviour, so it suits the start.

options.text: Surprise praise teaches this new act faster than steady praise.
options.feedback: A reward after each try teaches a new act fastest. Uneven rewards can help a learned response last.

items.stem: In a feed with variable rewards, each swipe has a 1-in-5 chance of a fun clip. After five swipes, what is the chance of at least one?

options.text: About 67%.
options.feedback: The chance of no clip five times is 0.8 to the fifth, about 33%, so at least one is about 67%.

options.text: 100%, since one in five means a clip by swipe five.
options.feedback: Chances do not stack that neatly. Five misses in a row can still happen.

options.text: 20%, the same as one swipe.
options.feedback: More swipes give more chances, so the total rises above one swipe's chance.

items.stem: At the train station, one machine gives a cup of chai each time a coin goes in. A lucky-draw box pays now and then. Both stop paying. Where will people keep trying longer?

options.text: At the chai machine, since it paid each time before.
options.feedback: When a reward that came each time stops, people notice fast and give up sooner.

options.text: At the lucky-draw box.
options.feedback: When rewards come at unknown times, a pause looks normal, so people keep trying there longer.

options.text: Both the same, since both stopped.
options.feedback: Both stopped, but uneven rewards fade much more slowly than steady ones.

items.stem: Zoya, a college student, turns off all like alerts, yet she still opens her chat app many times a day. Working back, what does that suggest?

options.text: Other pulls, like news from friends, keep her opening it.
options.feedback: Right. Surprise likes are one pull, but people also open apps for friends and news, so many things keep them coming back.

options.text: Surprise likes still explain her checks, even with alerts off.
options.feedback: People open apps for several reasons. Her checks can continue through other pulls, such as news from friends.

options.text: Surprise likes are the one reason people open apps.
options.feedback: If likes were the whole story, turning off alerts would end it. Friends, news and design also pull people back.

items.stem: Arjun says feeds are slot machines and no other thing keeps people scrolling. What is not quite right?

options.text: Surprise rewards are one pull among several.
options.feedback: Apps also use endless scroll and read ticks, and people come for friends and news.

options.text: Feeds pay out on a fixed count.
options.feedback: Feeds do not pay on a set count. The point is that rewards are only one pull.

options.text: Slot machines share no features with feeds.
options.feedback: They share uneven rewards. But feeds also use other hooks.

misconceptions.name: Every swipe rewards
misconceptions.correction: A good result can come after dull ones, with no set gap.

misconceptions.name: One cause explains all use
misconceptions.correction: People open feeds for many reasons, and apps use several hooks, not just uncertain rewards.

misconceptions.name: It is just willpower
misconceptions.correction: Rewards that come at unknown times keep checks going for most people, whatever their willpower.

misconceptions.name: A skipped reward is variable
misconceptions.correction: A reward after every fifth try is fixed; on a variable schedule, the number of tries keeps changing.

misconceptions.name: Surprise rewards teach fastest
misconceptions.correction: A reward after every try is the quickest way to teach a new act.

misconceptions.name: Steady rewards last longer
misconceptions.correction: Responses learned with uneven rewards are slower to fade when rewards stop.

steps.title: Variable means you cannot tell when

hook.stem: A game gives a prize after some rounds but not others, with no pattern. How would you describe these prizes?

options.text: They come at uneven times.
options.feedback: Right. When a reward comes at uneven, unknown times, it is called variable.

options.text: They come after every round.
options.feedback: Not every round pays. Some do and some do not, with no pattern.

options.text: They come every fifth round.
options.feedback: That would be a fixed pattern. Here the prize comes at uneven times.

steps.teach: With a variable reward, the tries before a prize keep changing, so you cannot tell which try will pay. A reward on every try teaches a new act fastest.

parts: Zubin keeps his phone on his desk,
and each time he opens his messages,
there might be a reply or nothing at all.
example.spot: there might be a reply or nothing at all.
example.feedback: Sometimes a reply, sometimes nothing, with no way to tell. That is a variable reward.

guided.stem: A teacher gives a gold star after every third homework. Is that a variable reward?
guided.hint: Can you tell when the star comes?

options.text: No, it is fixed.
options.feedback: Right. You know the star comes every third time, so it is fixed. A reward on every try teaches a new act fastest.

options.text: Yes, as it does not come each time.
options.feedback: Not every time is not the same as variable. You know it comes every third time, so it is fixed.

options.text: Yes, since some homework gets no star.
options.feedback: Missing some tries is not enough. The star comes every third time, so you can tell when: it is fixed.

guided.stem: Arjun is teaching his new puppy to sit. In the first week, when should a treat come to teach the act fastest?
guided.hint: What teaches a brand-new act quickest?

options.text: After every sit.
options.feedback: Right. A reward after every try is the quickest way to teach a new behaviour.

options.text: After a random number of sits, for suspense.
options.feedback: Uneven rewards keep a learned act going, but a reward after every try teaches a new act fastest.

options.text: After each fifth sit.
options.feedback: A reward on each try teaches fastest. Skipping tries slows the first learning.

guided.stem: Pradeep, a salesman in Rajkot, makes calls all day. Some calls end in a sale, with no pattern to which ones. How is his reward best described?
guided.hint: Can he tell in advance which call pays?

options.text: Fixed, since his salary comes each month.
options.feedback: The monthly salary is a different reward. For each call, the sales come at uneven times.

options.text: Variable, since the tries per sale keep changing.
options.feedback: Right. The number of calls before a sale keeps changing, so he cannot tell which call will pay.

options.text: Fixed, since a sale comes after a set number of calls.
options.feedback: There is no set number here. When the tries before a reward keep changing, the schedule is variable.

steps.takeaway: Variable means the reward comes, but you cannot tell when.

steps.title: Not knowing keeps you checking

hook.stem: A fishing spot gives a catch on some casts but not others, with no pattern. Why do people keep casting?

options.text: The next cast might bring a fish.
options.feedback: Right. No one can tell which cast will pay, so each new one seems worth a try.

options.text: Each cast brings a fish.
options.feedback: Most casts bring nothing. The pull is that the next one might.

options.text: Someone makes them keep casting.
options.feedback: Nobody forces them. Not knowing which cast pays keeps people casting.

steps.teach: When the next try might pay, it seems worth making, so people keep going. That is why habits built on such rewards are slow to fade.

parts: Nikita finds a funny meme only now and then,
so she keeps swiping
in case the next one is good.
example.spot: in case the next one is good.
example.feedback: Not knowing when the next good one comes keeps her swiping.

guided.stem: At the college library, a free newspaper sits on the front desk on some days but not others, with no pattern. Why does Imran check the desk every visit?
guided.hint: Can he tell ahead of time which days pay off?

options.text: Any visit might be the one with a paper.
options.feedback: Yes. He cannot tell which visit pays, so each check seems worth making.

options.text: A paper is there on every visit.
options.feedback: Papers turn up only on some days, with no pattern, so not every visit pays.

options.text: Visits with no paper make him stop checking.
options.feedback: Habits built on uneven rewards are slow to fade, so empty visits do not stop him.

guided.stem: Anil's cousin sends funny voice notes at random times. His boss sends one report at the end of each day. Which chat is Anil likely to check more often through the day?
guided.hint: Which one could have something new at any moment?

options.text: The boss's chat, since it matters more.
options.feedback: The boss's report comes at a known time, so there is no point checking early. Unknown timing drives checking.

options.text: Both the same, since he likes both.
options.feedback: Liking is not the driver. Not knowing when the next reward comes keeps people checking.

options.text: The cousin's chat.
options.feedback: Right. When a reward could come at any time, people keep checking at a high, steady rate.

guided.stem: A reporter in Patna gets a big story tip now and then from one source, with no pattern. The source moves away without saying so. What is most likely?
guided.hint: Can she tell that the next tip is not coming?

options.text: She keeps checking with the source for a long time.

concepts.title: If-then plans
concepts.hook: A plan tied to a clear moment can help turn a goal into an action.
concepts.rule: An if-then plan names a cue and the action to take when it appears. This link can help people start.

claims.text: An if-then plan spells out the when, where and how in advance: if situation Y comes, then I will do X.
Across 94 tests, if-then plans had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals, on average.
If-then plans make the named moment easier to spot and the response to it more automatic.
When a plan worked by sharpening the cue, other cues were more often passed over.
A 2025 review of 642 tests found if-then plans helped thinking, feelings and actions, with effects from small to medium-large.

steps.title: Link a moment to an action

concepts.title: The spotlight effect
concepts.hook: A small slip can feel huge to us. Others may notice it less.
concepts.rule: The spotlight effect means we guess that more people notice us than really do. Some still notice, and they tend to judge our slips more kindly than we fear.

claims.text: In two studies, people wearing a T-shirt with a striking image guessed that more people could recall it than really could.
In a group talk, speakers thought their good and bad remarks stood out more to others than they did.
After a public slip, people expected others to judge them more harshly than others really did.
People seem to start from their own rich view of a moment and adjust too little for how others see it.
The fear of harsh judgment came partly from people dwelling on their own mishap and forgetting what else onlookers take into account.

items.stem: Before a college viva, Sanjana gets a pimple on her nose and worries the panel will remember it. What is most likely?

options.text: Each panel member will recall it clearly.
options.feedback: That is the spotlight guess. Others notice and recall far less than we expect.

options.text: The panel will mark her down for it.
options.feedback: A viva is marked on answers. And few will even recall the pimple.

options.text: Few on the panel will recall it later.
options.feedback: People tend to overrate how much others notice them, so the panel will likely recall little.

items.stem: Made-up numbers: Arnav guessed 12 classmates would recall the picture on his bright shirt. His guess was 7 too high. How many could really recall it?

options.text: About 5.
options.feedback: If 12 was 7 too high, the real count is 12 minus 7, which is 5.

options.text: About 19.
options.feedback: That adds the 7 on. His guess was too high, so the real count is lower.

options.text: About 12.
options.feedback: That is his guess. The real count was 7 lower than that.

items.stem: In an online college class, Varsha's video freezes on a funny face for a few seconds. Because it felt huge to her, she says the whole class must have noticed. What is not quite right?

options.text: It felt huge because she lived it in full detail.
options.feedback: Right. She saw every second from the inside. Classmates caught a brief moment, so far fewer noticed than she thinks.

options.text: No slip; a big feeling means many noticed.
options.feedback: How big a moment feels to us says little about others. We live our own moments in close-up.

options.text: No classmate saw it, so her worry has no basis.
options.feedback: Some of the class may have seen it. She lived it up close, so she thinks more people saw it than did.

options.text: No; it covers embarrassing slips alone.
options.feedback: It is not limited to slips. Good remarks were also overrated.

options.text: Yes; we overrate how much good moments stand out too.
options.feedback: In the study, speakers overrated how much both good and bad remarks stood out.

options.text: No; clever points get remembered by everyone in the room later.
options.feedback: Others noticed both good and bad remarks less than speakers thought.

items.stem: Which line sums up what the slip studies found?

options.text: People were judged more harshly than they feared.
options.feedback: It went the other way. The fear was bigger than the real judgment.

options.text: No onlooker took note of the slips.
options.feedback: Some people can notice a slip. The studies found that feared judgment was harsher than the judgment received.

options.text: People feared harsher judgment than they got.
options.feedback: Across four studies, people expected to be judged more harshly than they were.

items.stem: Yash drops his tray on the wet canteen floor. He replays it all night and fears everyone thinks he is clumsy. Both errors come from ___.

options.text: living the slip up close and missing the wet floor
options.feedback: Right. Seen from the inside, the slip looms large, and fixing on it hides the wet floor that onlookers saw.

options.text: other students staring at him all night
options.feedback: Onlookers glance and move on. The night of replays comes from his own close-up view of the slip.

options.text: other students judging him harshly despite the wet floor
options.feedback: People can judge a slip more kindly than expected and take context into account. He is dwelling on the mishap.

misconceptions.correction: Our own vivid view can make an event seem more visible to others than it was.

misconceptions.correction: Some people may take note. The guess is often too high.

misconceptions.correction: After a slip, people judged us more kindly than we expected.

misconceptions.name: Only embarrassing moments
misconceptions.correction: We also overrate how much our good moments stand out to others.

guided.stem: On a quiz stage, Tina flubs a question that the other teams also missed. She fears the hall thinks she is slow. What do onlookers more likely think?
guided.hint: What do onlookers see that the speaker forgets?

options.text: That it was a hard question.
options.feedback: Yes. Onlookers weigh the whole situation, such as a hard question, so they judge more kindly than she fears.

options.text: That she is slow, just as she fears.
options.feedback: After a slip, people expect harsher judgment than they get. Onlookers also weigh how hard the question was.

options.text: That she is even slower than she fears.
options.feedback: It runs the other way. Others judge slips more kindly than people fear, and they see the hard question.

guided.stem: Arjun forgets a line in a school play and spends the night on that one moment. His mother remembers the whole show and the stuffy hall. Why does he expect a harsher view than she holds?
guided.hint: What does each of them focus on?

options.text: She is being kind to spare his feelings.
options.feedback: Kindness was not the finding. Onlookers really judged slips more kindly, because they weigh the whole scene.

options.text: He dwells on one moment.
options.feedback: Right. Dwelling on our own slip makes us forget what else onlookers weigh, so we expect harsh judgment.

options.text: He is right; one slip sinks a whole show.
options.feedback: Onlookers weighed the whole situation, so one slip mattered less to them than he expects.

guided.stem: Gauri's card machine fails while a queue waits at her shop in Indore. She expects buyers to think her shop is badly run. What do they more likely weigh?
guided.hint: What do onlookers see that she forgets?

options.text: That the shop should have had a spare machine.
options.feedback: Onlookers tend to judge a slip more kindly than feared. Most see a common machine fault, not a planning failure.

options.text: Nobody saw it, so it does not matter.
options.feedback: Some buyers did see it. The point is that they judged it more kindly than she fears.

options.text: That card machines fail at times.
options.feedback: Right. Onlookers weigh the whole situation, so they judge a slip more kindly than the person fears.

steps.takeaway: Others usually judge our slips more kindly than we fear.
